s1.syndrome_frame: A subacute to chronic, painful, crusted, erythematous skin lesion on the chest
salient_findings: Large, crusted, erythematous plaque on the right chest
Painful area on the right lateral chest
key_facts: Female patient in her 50s
2-week history of a painful area on the right lateral chest
Taking prednisone, 10 mg, daily
Previous treatments included methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, glycopyrrolate, oral antibiotics, topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, and topical antibiotics
Biopsy was previously performed
Laboratory values within normal limits for intact parathyroid hormone, ionized calcium, and phosphorus

shortlist.label: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
shortlist.why_kept: subacute to chronic, painful skin lesion

shortlist.label: Squamous cell carcinoma
shortlist.why_kept: crusted, erythematous plaque on the chest

shortlist.label: Eczematous dermatitis
shortlist.why_kept: previous treatments with topical corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors

shortlist.label: Psoriasis
shortlist.why_kept: erythematous plaque on the chest, despite normal laboratory values

raw.rationale: The patient's history of a painful, crusted, erythematous plaque, along with a history of unsuccessful treatments with various medications, is consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum, a condition known for its ulcerative and painful skin lesions that are often resistant to treatment.

rejected.label: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
rejected.why: While possible, the lack of specific biopsy results and the description of the lesion does not strongly suggest this diagnosis.

rejected.label: Squamous cell carcinoma
rejected.why: The description of the lesion as a crusted, erythematous plaque does not specifically suggest squamous cell carcinoma, and biopsy results are not detailed.

rejected.label: Eczematous dermatitis
rejected.why: The patient's history of unsuccessful treatment with topical corticosteroids and other typical eczema treatments makes this less likely.

rejected.label: Psoriasis
rejected.why: The description of the lesion and the patient's response to previous treatments does not strongly support a diagnosis of psoriasis.
